title: Two dimensions of optimization: context and behavior

opening.headline: When a model is wrong, we establish standards to distinguish whether the cause is due to ignorance or a misguided method.
body: If the model's response is incorrect, it is usually logged as a problem with the same name. However, answers that are incorrect due to not knowing the latest policy and answers that know the policy but do not follow the requested format have different causes. If the cause is different, the method of fixing it must also be different.

In this lesson, we will divide model optimization into two axes: context and behavior. We follow the process of placing failure cases on two axes and even organize the order in which optimization should be repeated.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the difference between lack of context and behavioral/formal issues
Failure cases can be classified into context axis and action axis.

screens.title: The model is wrong, but why?
screens.lead: First, read two examples of failures that pile up one team's bug list. It is good to read while thinking about whether both cases can be fixed in the same way.

visual.alt: A scene where two incorrect response cards for different reasons are combined into one bug list.
labels: Card A: Answer with old policy
When asked about the new refund policy, confidently answer the previous policy.
The policy is correct, but the answer is in line text instead of JSON.
Can it be fixed with the same prescription?

paragraphs: We have a team that runs a customer support chatbot. Two failures were reported in one day. The first is when the model confidently answers the previous policy when asked about the new refund policy. The second is a case where the policy content was stated accurately, but the answer was given in line text instead of the requested JSON format.

Both cases were logged as 'Invalid Model' and piled into the same bug ticket. After that, the prompts are lengthened, documents are attached, and even tuning attempts occur in no particular order. Some efforts work, some just cost money. Why is that so?

The reason is that failure was viewed as a lump. If we cannot distinguish whether the reason the model is wrong is because we do not know or because of the method, the prescriptions will be mixed. OpenAI's accuracy optimization guide suggests looking at this problem along two axes. He then explains that they must first decide which lever to pull.
In this class, we will sequentially look at what the two axes are, how to classify failure cases, and the order in which improvement is repeated after classification.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: What happens if you write the same prescription on Card A and Card B? By the end of class, you will be able to answer this question with evidence.

screens.outro: Let me start by recalling an example from your own experience.

screens.title: Think of a recent mistake
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit an answer, so think of the case in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Think of a recent example where the model was wrong. What input did it come from, and which part was wrong?
items.answer: When recalling examples, it is important to remember both inputs and outputs. This is because even if the answer is the same, the cause is completely different depending on whether the information required for input was included. We'll reclassify the cases you've come up with in the following screens, so keep them in mind.

items.prompt: Was the reason the answer was wrong because they didn't know the information or because the method was wrong?
items.answer: If you have guessed the answer in your head, it's okay. This is not a question with a correct answer. Just think about what the basis for your guess was. The evidence that ‘the model is unlikely to have seen the information’ refers to a problem with the information, and the evidence that ‘there is information, but the format or tone was different’ points to a problem with the method.

items.prompt: What have you tried to do to fix that failure? Was that attempt appropriate for the cause?
items.answer: Many teams look at increasing prompts, attaching documentation, or tuning as they see it. If the cause and prescription are correct, the effect is great, but if they are not, it only costs time and money. The goal of this class is to get you into the habit of sorting out causes before choosing a treatment.

screens.outro: Now that we have prepared the case, let us identify the two axes that divide failure.

screens.title: Two axes: context and action
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare how the symptoms, causes, and representative prescriptions of the two axes differ. Also check the horizontal and vertical axes of the picture.

visual.alt: A 2x2 diagram with context on the horizontal axis and action on the vertical axis, with an explanatory panel on the right.
labels: Contextual Optimization: What the Model Knows

tabs.label: Context Axis: The Unknown Problem
tabs.body:
**Symptom**: The model confidently states things that are not true, or is completely unaware of recent events or company information.

**Cause**: The OpenAI guide describes three cases where context optimization is needed: First, when the information was not in the training data. Second, when the knowledge of the model becomes outdated. Third, there are times when information that the model does not know, such as company-private information, is needed.

**Goal**: This axis increases the accuracy of responses.

**Representative prescription**: Find the information you need and put it into the prompt. You can paste it statically, or you can use Search Augmentation (RAG) to import the data you need for each question. To use an analogy, it is the method of opening a textbook, finding the answer, and writing it down.

tabs.label: Action Axis: Problems that can't be done
tabs.body:
**Symptom**: Sufficient information is provided, but the format of the output is jagged, the tone and style are different from expectations, or established reasoning procedures are not consistently followed.

**Cause**: The OpenAI guide describes three cases where LLM optimization is needed. First, the results are inconsistent and poorly formatted. Second, the tone or style of speech does not match. Third, the reasoning pattern is not consistently followed.

**Goal**: This axis increases consistency of behavior.

**Representative prescription**: Clear instructions and show examples first, and if it is repeated, consider fine tuning to learn the same behavior. To use an analogy, it is a method that you learn by taking classes for several months.

tabs.label: Parable of two memories
tabs.body:
The OpenAI guide suggests splitting each failure into whether it's a memory issue in context or a learned memory issue.

**in-context memory** is like having a textbook nearby and looking up the parts you need. This is solved by putting relevant information into the context window for the model.

**Learned memory** is like solving the same type of problem over and over again for six months. The model is shown examples of input and expected responses and trained to solve the problem.

These two methods have an additive relationship. They are not mutually exclusive, so for some use cases, best performance is achieved when both are used together.

tabs.label: Why split the axis?
tabs.body:
Many guides describe optimization as a straight staircase leading from prompt, search, and tune. But the OpenAI guide says this is often not the case. The three are levers that solve different problems, so you need to pull the right lever to get going in the right direction.

So it's useful to think of optimization as a matrix. I usually start with the engineering prompt in the bottom left to get a baseline. Only after looking at the wrong case and understanding why it was wrong can you decide whether to go to the context axis or the action axis.

screens.outro: Now that we have defined the axes, let's put an actual failure example on this diagram.

screens.title: The process of placing failure cases on axes
screens.lead: The table below shows the results of placing four failure cases on two axes, one each. Read each row from top to bottom, noting that the same questions are asked repeatedly.

data.caption: Classification process for four failure cases
columns: Was there any information needed to be entered?
Basis for judgment and first prescription
rows: Answered the price of a new product incorrectly
There wasn't. This is information the model never had.

A model cannot tell you information it has not seen. Refining instructions doesn't help, so finding a price list and inserting context into the input is the first remedy. In this case, no matter how long you trim the prompt, you won't be able to get an answer if the fact that it's a price is not included in the input.
The order of requested fields keeps changing and output
It's not an information problem, but a problem with the output method being unstable. First, specify the field order and show an example. If it is still repeated, consider tuning it.
You know the policy, but you break the polite tone guidelines.
There was. The policy content is accurately contained in the answer.
It's a tone issue because the content is correct and the wording is incorrect. Provide tone guidelines and examples of good responses, and review ways to train tone when repeated.
I attached a document, but used the wrong paragraph as the basis.
We don't know yet. You need to check what context was entered.
If the wrong paragraph is included, the search or selection was incorrect. Before making a decision, we check what actually went into the model input.
data.notes: The classification question is always the same. Was the information needed for this response included in the input, or was it done in a wrong way? After classification, the number of failure types is accumulated to reveal which axis has the biggest problem. In the four cases above, there is one case on the context axis, two cases on the action axis, and one case that requires confirmation. This table is also an exercise in asking the same questions one at a time. If you only change the case without changing the question, failures can be classified using the same criteria even if the person in charge is different, and the classification results can be read together by the team. Also, in cases where it is difficult to enter in any box, it is safer to first check what was entered rather than forcefully classifying it. If you record the classification results, they will serve as data to later compare the rates by failure type.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the classification criteria, let's unravel two sentences that are easily confusing with explanation.

screens.title: Commentary: ‘Do not know the latest information’ and ‘Do not follow the format’
screens.lead: The instructor explains the two sentences in the same order. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step. Learners do not enter answers.

steps.title: Step 1: Read the symptoms as they are
steps.body: Both sentences start with 'the model is wrong'. Sentence At this stage, we don't think about solutions, we just check what's wrong with the response. The content of X is wrong, and the shape of Y is wrong, not the content.

steps.title: Step 2: Ask if the input contains information
steps.body: X's input is not up to date. Since the model cannot know what will happen after learning has finished, no matter how you instruct it, it will not be able to come up with an answer. Y's input already has the information it needs. The model knows the content, but cannot present it in the requested way.

steps.title: Step 3: Determine the axis
steps.body: X is the context axis and Y is the behavioral axis. It's the same 'wrong', but it's a problem that one side doesn't know and the other side can't do. Only after making this decision can you decide which lever to pull.

steps.title: Step 4: Choose the first prescription for each axis
steps.body: X's first prescription is to inject context by finding relevant material and putting it into the prompt. This is because no matter how much you refine the instructions, you cannot come up with an answer without supporting data. Y's first prescription is to make instructions clear and show examples. If this is resolved, it will be the cheapest solution.

steps.title: Step 5: See what happens if the prescription is violated
steps.body: If you use tuning on Adding Y to search makes the material richer, but the format is still shaky. If the cause and treatment are mismatched, the same failure will remain, only costing money.

steps.title: Step 6: Repeated failure takes it one step further
steps.body: If Y is not resolved even with instructions and examples and is repeated, consider tuning to learn the behavior at that time. This judgment should be based on evaluation results, not on feelings. The next screen covers that sequence. For example, if formatting errors continue to occur at the same rate even after reinforcing the same instructions multiple times and including examples, this may not be a problem with the prompt but rather a signal that the behavior needs to be learned.

screens.outro: Now that you know how to choose a regimen, let's look at what order you should repeat them.

screens.title: Optimization sequence: evaluation first, one lever at a time
screens.lead: When you select and expand each item, the purpose of each step and what to check will appear. Spread them out in order from top to bottom.

visual.alt: Flowchart showing the cycle of evaluation, hypothesis, application, and re-evaluation, with an example flow on the right.

items.title: 1. Write an evaluation first
items.body: The iterative flow presented by the OpenAI guide starts with writing an evaluation. Without a device to measure whether your output meets your standards, you won't know if you've improved. The Anthropic document also advises setting specific and measurable success criteria and designing evaluations. If the criteria are vague, no prescription can be proven effective.

items.title: 2. Establish a baseline with prompts
items.body: Start with the simplest prompt and expected output. These results will serve as a baseline against which all future improvements will be compared. The biggest output of this step is looking at examples of baseline failures and developing hypotheses about why they were wrong.

items.title: 3. Apply one lever that fits your hypothesis
items.body: If the hypothesis is a context issue, context injection or retrieval is addressed first, and if the hypothesis is a behavioral issue, instructions and examples are addressed first. The important thing at this stage is to change only one thing at a time. If you change several things at the same time, you won't know which change had an effect.

items.title: 4. Re-evaluate and decide on the next lever
items.body: Measure again with the same assessment to see if there has been improvement. If it works, keep it and reclassify any remaining failures. Since the lever is not a straight staircase but a matrix that solves different problems, the next lever is determined by the evaluation results.

items.title: 5. Representative repetitive flow example
items.body: The example from the OpenAI guide continues like this. We start with a prompt and then evaluate it. Increase consistency by including static few-shot examples. Add a search and dynamically insert examples that match your question. We prepare and tune more than 50 examples. Finally, we refine our search and add additional fact-checking steps. It's about taking only the necessary steps, and not all problems go down this road.

screens.outro: In the final screen, we will group today's key points into one standard.

screens.title: What you don't know, turn to context, and what you don't know, turn to action.
screens.lead: Go back to the question asked at the beginning of class and organize what you learned today into a single judgment standard.

paragraphs: Let me recall the first two cases I saw. Card A is a case of the old policy being the answer, so the model has never seen the new policy, so it's a problem on the context axis. Card B is a case where the policy is correct but the format is violated. There is information but the method is shaky, so it is a problem on the action axis. If you use the same prescription for two cases, one will inevitably incur costs and fail.

The two axes can be organized like this. The context axis increases the accuracy of responses, and the action axis increases consistency of behavior. Context is handled by putting information into context, and behavior is handled by instructions, examples, and learning when necessary.

The first question in classification is always the same. Was the information needed for this response included in the input, or was it done in a wrong way? With this question, we first divide the failure and then choose a remedy.

After deciding on a prescription, set the evaluation criteria first and repeat, changing one lever at a time. There is no need to decide the order by feel, because the evaluation results inform you of the next lever.

This framework serves as the foundation for subsequent learning. When looking at problems that can be solved by prompting, problems that can be solved by searching, and problems that can be solved by tuning, we first ask on which axis the problem lies.

callout.label: Based on one sentence
callout.text: Solve what you don't know through context, what you can't figure out through action, and change one lever at a time while looking at the evaluation results.

checks.intro: Check for yourself by recalling the classification process you just saw. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: I attached a document to the prompt, but the model answered based on the wrong paragraph. What is the first thing to do before deciding on an axis?
options: Check what context actually entered the model input
Collect the same cases and immediately create tuning data.
Rewrite the instructions to be longer and observe the results.
Confirm it as a behavior axis problem and add a formal example
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. The basis for classification is whether there is information in the input, so you must first check the input content.
checks.incorrectFeedback: It's a pity. If you choose a treatment first without determining the cause, the same failure will remain.
checks.explain: This case is a case of context axis suspicion where you need to check what context was entered into the input. The basis for classification is whether there is information in the input.

wrong.1: If you start tuning without knowing what went into the input, you may end up with the same failure.
wrong.2: If you only modify the instructions before checking the input, you will not be able to determine the cause.
wrong.3: If you decide on the behavioral axis before confirming the cause, the prescription will be wrong.

checks.intro: Recall the two sentences you saw in the commentary and pair the failure situation with the first prescription. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Match failure situations with remedies to try first
left: I don't know the latest information because there is no supporting data in the input.
The information is there, but the output format is shaky.
Even if instructions and examples are refined, formatting failures are repeated.
right: Inject context by finding relevant material and putting it in the prompt
checks.correctFeedback: The first prescriptions for all three situations have been linked appropriately.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The prescription for some situations was off. Again, try to distinguish between lack of information and shaky methods.
checks.explain: If there is no information, context is injected. If there is information but the method is shaky, instructions and examples come first. If it is still repeated, tuning is considered.

checks.intro: Think about the flow of repeating optimization and put them in order. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Put the optimization iteration flow suggested by the OpenAI guide in order.
checks.correctFeedback: The order of starting from evaluation and returning to evaluation was set exactly.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is incorrect. Recall that you must first have an assessment to compare the baseline to.
checks.explain: You must first have an evaluation standard so you can compare the baseline and the amount of improvement, and you must change one lever at a time to find out the cause of the effect.

glossary.def: It's a matter of whether the input contains the information the model needs to know. Addresses lack of current information, private information, and information that was not studied and improves response accuracy.
It's a matter of how the model handles the information. It promotes consistency of behavior by addressing whether output format, tone, and reasoning procedures are consistently followed.
You answer by looking at the material provided in the prompt. It can be compared to opening a textbook and unraveling it.
This is a method that learns by repeating examples of input and expected responses to learn through action. Fine tuning applies here.
This is a device that repeatedly measures whether the model’s output meets established standards. This provides the basis for judging which improvements were effective.

misconceptions.myth: If the model is wrong, replace it with a larger model.
misconceptions.fact: Problems with insufficient information and problems with inconsistent methods have different causes. Changing the model is often not a prescription, so you first need to sort out which axis the problem is.

misconceptions.myth: Optimization is a straight staircase that leads to prompting, discovery, and tuning.
misconceptions.fact: The three are levers that solve different problems. The results and evaluation of the failure triage determine which lever to pull next.

misconceptions.myth: You should only use one of the two: search and tuning.
misconceptions.fact: The two methods are additive. In use cases where both contextual and behavioral issues exist, the two are sometimes used together.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Solve what you don't know through context, and what you can't figure out through action.
The context axis increases the accuracy of responses, and the action axis increases consistency of behavior.
Failure cases are first classified based on whether the information needed to be entered was present, and then a prescription is selected.
Set the evaluation criteria first and repeat, changing one lever at a time.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Is our team's recent failure closer to the context axis or the action axis, and what is the basis for that judgment?
